questions.q: When a producer supplies a partition key, what guarantee does that buy, per this lesson?
options: Every message with that same key always lands on the same partition, guaranteeing per-key ordering
The message is guaranteed to be delivered to every consumer group at once
The message is written to every partition for redundancy
The key is stripped out before the message reaches any partition
questions.explain: hash(key) % numPartitions always maps the same key to the same partition, which is what makes per-key ordering possible.

questions.q: What happens when a producer sends a message with no key at all?
options: Kafka spreads messages round-robin across partitions — even load, but no ordering guarantee tied to any value
Kafka refuses to accept the message
The message is always sent to partition 0
Kafka assigns a random key automatically that consumers can read
questions.explain: Without a key, distribution is even, but nothing ties a set of related messages to the same partition anymore.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the practical ceiling on parallelism when a topic has too few partitions?
options: A consumer group can never have more actively working consumers than there are partitions — extras just sit idle
There is no ceiling; more consumers always increase throughput
Too few partitions causes Kafka to reject new consumers outright
Partition count has no relationship to consumer parallelism
questions.explain: Since a partition is read by only one consumer per group at a time, partition count is a hard ceiling on parallel consumption.

questions.q: Why does keying by "country" risk creating a hot partition, per this lesson's example?
options: Because if traffic is heavily skewed toward one country, that key's low cardinality sends most load to a single partition
Because "country" is not a valid data type for a partition key
Because Kafka has a specific rule banning geographic partition keys
Because it causes every message to be duplicated across all partitions
questions.explain: The hash spreads load evenly only if the key values themselves are reasonably even — a skewed, low-cardinality key breaks that assumption.

questions.q: What is a concrete downside of having far too many partitions, according to this lesson?
options: More open file handles per broker, slower leader elections and rebalances, and more replication traffic for the same total data
Kafka automatically deletes topics that exceed a partition limit
Producers can no longer supply a partition key
Consumers are limited to reading from only one partition ever
questions.explain: Every partition is real per-broker overhead — it isn't a free way to future-proof parallelism.
